quotes.verbatim_quote:
We can improvise over any chord or any sequence of chords belonging to any harmonic
;ield simply by using the Ionian or Aeolian Mode of the key we are in. We call this approach
"key improvising" or "key improvisation". We will go deeper into the other modes later in
our studies. For now, we will create the sounds of all the modes using the Ionian and
Aeolian scales.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Central thesis: Ionian + Aeolian cover all seven harmonic field modes.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
Be careful with the avoid notes of both scales (perfect 4th in the Ionian mode, and ;lat 6th

quotes.why_load_bearing: Names avoid notes for both scales.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
In the key of “C”, the avoid note will be “F”, which should not be used
over Cmaj7 or Am7. But remember that there are always exceptions and at times the avoid
note works ;ine depending on the situation.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Concrete example + contextual exception to the avoid-note rule.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
So in the beginning we will learn simple melodic patterns that will help us get familiar with both
scales, DO NOT rely on these. Remember these are only exercises and can sound very predictable.
This is the first step on the long road that we have ahead of us.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Warns against mechanically internalizing patterns; they are first step only.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
Note: As the following pattern exercises were built using “C” Ionian and “A” Aeolian, they
can also be played over any chord or sequence belonging to “C” Natural Major Harmonic
Field or “A” Natural Minor Harmonic Field.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Extends each exercise's scope from one chord to a whole harmonic field.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
One of the most dif-icult things for guitar player, is to master the scales and other melodic
ideas all over the guitar fretboard. The reason for this is because the fingerings constantly
change from one position to another. So in order to solve this problem, let’s split the fretboard
into -ive vertical zones. It is important to understand that the vertical visualization is the
key to playing horizontally, because it makes it possible to connect the fretboard zones
going from one to another without getting lost. In other words, we visualize vertically but
play horizontally most of the time.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Signature five-zone system; visualize vertically, play horizontally.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
Let’s start visualizing the Ionian and Aeolian scale (key & relative scale) in the five vertical
zones. Each zone will be related with a chord shape (Cmaj7 or Am7). The chords will guide
us better then just single notes, because they are -ixed structures, which are easier to
remember rather than a lot of single notes. Make sure to use the root of each chord to
guide you in each zone.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Anchor scale zones to chord shapes for memory.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
Attention:
Usually, the vertical ideas do not work as well as the horizontal ideas. However, we have some
exceptions, and sometimes both work perfectly. Next we have many examples of Ionian and
Aeolian scales vertically and horizontally. Choose the examples you like the most, memorize
them and have fun.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Explicit stylistic preference for horizontal over vertical.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
As we have learned, the natural harmonic scale, also known as the Ionian Mode, is the
mother of six other scales and together they form the seven harmonic ;ield modes. We will
concentrate on the two related modes, Ionian and Aeolian. We will summarize the seven
scales of the harmonic ;ields into these two scales.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Ionian as generative root; justifies the two-scale teaching scope.
